newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Weak regional demand pressures Sept LSWR prices.
newsitem.headline: Weak regional demand pressures Sept LSWR prices.

text.p: Low sulphur waxy residue (LSWR) prices for Asian cargoes lifting in September are coming under pressure as regional demand falters, traders said on Wednesday.
"There are more than enough barrels to cover demand," said a Japanese trader. "There may be as much as 1.5 million barrels surplus."

Industry sources said they estimated regional demand in September would be around 2.71 million barrels with 1.2 million barrels required by Japan, 500,000 barrels by South Korea, 250,000 barrels for Taiwan, 200,000 barrels for India and the
usual term supply of 560,000 barrels to Italy.
"Japanese demand for the summer season is already over," said a Japanese trader. "It peaked in July and August."
Japanese utilities are the region's major LSWR consumers, using it for electricity generation.
But Japanese LSWR demand is also being cut as the utilities, encouraged by the Japanese government, are moving increasingly towards cleaner fuel gas, Japanese traders said.

Ample supplies and a weak price for Indonesia's benchmark Minas crude in September could also undermine LSWR if utilities decide to burn the low sulphur crude instead of LSWR, the traders said. Minas was assessed below $19.00 per barrel for September liftings, traders said.

Traders said the price for Indonesia's cracked LSWR lifting in September had fallen by Wednesday to 50 cents over its base formula compared with a 75-cent peak premium for August barrels. Indonesia is Asia's biggest exporter of LSWR.
Last week LSWR was being assessed as high as $18.00 per barrel on an outright basis, which one trader said was $1.00 too high.
Since, prices have fallen to around $17.50 per barrel.
Last week Pertamina allocated 3.6 million barrels for September export liftings.
But traders said other regional exporters, Singapore and Malaysia, have 200,000 barrels and 340,000 barrels respectively of straight run LSWR for export.
The arbitrage into the U.S. market, an alternative outlet for excess Asian barrels for either burning in the winter season or cracking, is shut.
"The U.S. feedstock market is very sluggish since cracker problems saw Venezuela dumping a lot of VGO (vacuum gas oil) into the market," said a trader with U.S. refiner.
"Prices of Indonesia LSWR are being assessed too high to work to the U.S.," he said.
